On modern instruments the soundboard is usually spruce or cedar, the back, sides and neck mostly mahogany or rosewood, and the fretboard rosewood, maple or ebony; American hardwoods such as walnut, oak, cherry and apple are also common. It is sounded with the fingers, a pick or a striker, mostly in solo playing or at folk gatherings.

The body runs along the soundboard, and there are usually three or four strings, with the fretboard mostly fretted to the natural scale. The player sounds it with a pick, the fingers or a small stick in the strumming hollow of the body; early on it was mostly used at small family gatherings and folk occasions.

As for range, the source says only that the frets are mostly laid out in the whole-tone scale and that twelve to sixteen are common. It is not loud and suits small family gatherings; it once served as a parlour instrument, and the source does not describe how the volume is controlled. Unlike a struck zither it is not hammered with mallets but plucked; it can be tuned with wooden friction pegs or metal tuners.

Research after 1980 reconstructed its development from old instruments, dividing it into transition, traditional and revival phases. Around 1880 the Kentucky maker Thomas began building and selling them, and because they were quiet they were mostly used at family gatherings. They were still rare through the first half of the twentieth century; in the 1950s Ritchie's performances in New York carried the instrument into the urban folk revival, and in the 1960s Fariña and others made it better known; in 1969 the Capritaurus company began mass production, switching to metal tuners and enlarging the body.
